Obviate

OB-vee-ayt · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To obviate is to make unnecessary or prevent, especially by acting ahead of time.

The new online portal obviated the need for parents to drive to the school office just to update an address.

Worked Example

Because the two companies had already agreed on every major term in private meetings, the formal negotiation session was largely obviated -- there was almost nothing left to discuss.

The negotiation wasn't cancelled by force; it simply became unnecessary because the real work was already done. That's the special flavor of obviate -- it removes the need for something, rather than blocking or defeating it.

How Strong Is It? — reduce → obviate → eliminate

reduce vs. obviate

reduce vs. obviate: To reduce a need is to lessen it somewhat, a smaller change than removing it entirely.

eliminate vs. obviate

eliminate vs. obviate: To eliminate a need is to erase it completely, just as total as obviate but a more everyday word for it.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — ob-

prefix — ob-: in the way of, against (Latin)

root — via

root — via: way, road (Latin)

suffix — -te (-ate)

suffix — -te (-ate): verb ending: to make (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Obviate comes from Latin ob- ('in the way of') plus via ('road, way') and the -ate verb ending (spelled -te here, sharing its a with via) -- literally 'to get in the way of' something before it happens, which came to mean heading off the need for it entirely.

Use the root in a new word: deviate

Use the root in a new word: deviate: The pilot had to deviate from the planned route to avoid the storm.

Root Check

Word Choice

Obviate is a formal, almost technical word -- you'll often see it in legal, business, or policy writing ('this policy obviates the need for...') rather than in casual conversation. Unlike thwart or stymie, which describe blocking something already in motion, obviate works earlier -- it removes the need for something before it ever becomes an issue.
